questions.html: Schrodinger owns a beautiful cat called Meow who loves to wear socks on its four feet. Schrodinger has a collection of many cat socks in three colours: white, red and yellow. What is the least number of socks Schrodinger must pull out from the drawer to guarantee getting four socks of matching colour?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 5)

Apply the Pigeon-hole principle.

1. Determine the Worst-Case Scenario:

To guarantee four socks of the same color, consider the worst-case scenario where Schrodinger pulls out socks in such a way that maximizes the number of socks needed before achieving four of any single color.

2. Calculate the Maximum Number of Socks Without Four of the Same Color:
If Schrodinger pulls out 3 socks of each color (which is 3 white, 3 red, and 3 yellow), that totals 9 socks, and still doesn't guarantee four of any color.

3. Add one more sock to Guarantee Four of the Same Color: By pulling out one more sock (which would be the 10th sock), Schrodinger will ensure that one of the colors reaches four socks. This is because, with the 10th sock, there will be at least four socks of one of the colors.

Thus, Schrodinger must pull out 10 socks to guarantee that at least four socks of one color are included.

questions.html:
Piyush is taking the DVRUO Classes Test Series' Discrete Mathematics test which consists of 5 dreadful MSQs (multiple select questions). Each MSQ has 5 options A, B, C, D and E. In a MSQ question, one or more than one options out of the five options is/are correct. In how many ways can Piyush write his answers for the test, assuming that he writes at least one option in each MSQ question.
Note that the order of the options in his answer of a question does not matter, for example, $\mathrm{ABC}, \mathrm{ACB}$ and $\mathrm{BCA}$ are considered the same answer. Also, the order in which he answers the questions, does not matter.
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 12)

For each MSQ question, Piyush has 31 ways (i.e. $2^{\wedge} 5-1$ ).
Let's find out the number of ways to answer a particular MSQ question:
- Each MSQ has 5 options: A, B, C, D, and E.
- Piyush must choose at least one option to include in his answer.
- The order of the options doesn't matter.

Since the order doesn't matter, for each option, Piyush has two choices: either include it in his answer or not include it.

For each MSQ, there are 5 options, so there are $2^{\wedge} 5$ possible combinations of including or not including each option. However, one of these combinations is the scenario where Piyush chooses none of the options, which we need to exclude.

Thus, the number of valid combinations where Piyush chooses at least one option is:
$2^{\wedge} 5-1=32-1=31$

Therefore, each MSQ question has 31 ways to answer it; So, for 5 question, answer is  $31^5.$

An old man climbs $12$ stairs. While climbing the stairs, he can take $1$-stair or $2$-stairs at a time, But he can't take two $2$-stairs consecutively.

In how many ways can this person climb the $12$ stairs?
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 19)

We have only one constraint -: "He can't take 2-stairs consecutively"

Case 1: when no 2-stairs at a time -: (12 1-stair and 0 2-stairs)

         11111.....11(12 times). Possible way = 1.

Case 2: (10 1-stair and 1 2-stairs)

         _1_1_1_1_1_1_1_1_1_1_  (underscore denotes possible places for 2-stairs at a time). Possible ways = 11C1

Case 3: (8 1-stair and 2 2-stairs) 

         _1_1_1_1_1_1_1_1_. Possible ways = 9C2

Case 4: (6 1-stair and 3 2-stairs)

         _1_1_1_1_1_1_. Possible ways = 7C3

Case 5: (4 1-stair and 4 2-stairs)

            _1_1_1_1_. Possible ways = 5C4

Case 6: (2 1-stair and 5 2-stairs) 

           Not possible (because there would be consecutive 2-stairs step)

Total possible ways = 1 + 11C1 + 9C2 + 7C3 +5C4 = 88

 

Source solution 2 (score: 13)

Assume $f(n)$ is the number of ways to climb $n$ stairs if the person climbing the stairs can take one stair or two stairs at a time But can't make two $2$-stairs consecutively.
$$
f(n)=f(n-1)+f(n-3)
$$

Let's understand the number of ways to climb $n$ stairs, which we denote by $f(n)$:

1. If the old man takes 1-stair first, then there are $f(n-1)$ ways to climb $n$ stairs.

2. If the old man takes 2-stairs first, then next he must take 1-stair because he can't take two 2-stairs consecutively, So, there are $f(n-3)$ ways to climb $n$ stairs in this case.

So, $ f(n)=f(n-1)+f(n-3) $

Where $f(1)=1, f(2)=2, f(3)=3$

So, $f(12)=88$

questions.html:
Let $\mathrm{G}$ be a finite group.

Which of the following statements are true?

options.html: The number of elements $x$ of $\text{G}$ such that $x^3=e$ is odd.
The number of elements $x$ of $\text{G}$ such that $x^3=e$ is even.
The number of elements $x$ of $\text{G}$ such that $x^2 \neq e$ is odd.
The number of elements $x$ of $\text{G}$ such that $x^2 \neq e$ is even.

questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C, D, E

Source solution 1 (score: 8)

A similar question in GATE:

  • https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ewdz0FQJ14w&list=PLIPZ2_p3RNHhXves0XVa8d5O6F4rUi3KR&index=18
MUST Watch above video solution, then read the following explanation.
 

The number of elements $x$ of G such that $x^3=e$ is  $\cdots$ 

$$ x^3 = e $$

# CASE 1: $x=e$

If $x$ is the identity element then it will always satisfy the above equation

$e^3 = e*e*e = e$

$ herefore$ No. of element such that $x = e$ and following $x^3 = e$ is 1

 

# CASE 2: $x eq e$

$x^3 = e$

$x^2*x=e$

$ herefore$ We get $x^{-1} = x^2$ and $(x^2)^{-1} = x$ using the property of inverse

OR

$<x> = \{x^1,x^2,x^3\} = \{x,x^2,e\} = <x^2>$

As we know that if $a^n = e$ then $a^{-1} = a^{n-1}$ in a finite group.

$ herefore$ We get $x^{-1} = x^2$ and $(x^2)^{-1} = x$

 

$ ecause$ $x$ and $x^2$ are DISTINCT and exist in pair

$ herefore$ No. of element such that $x eq e$ and following $x^3 = e$ is EVEN

 

From both the cases the no. of element $x$ of G such that $x^3 = e$

= 1 + EVEN 

= ODD

 

$ herefore $ Option “A” is CORRECT and Option “B” is INCORRECT.

ANSWER = { A: ✅, B: ❌, C: ❔, D: ❔}

 

The number of elements $x$ of G such that $x^2 eq e$ is  $\cdots$ 

$$x^2 eq e$$

Let’s understand what $x^2 = e$ means first

$x^2 = x*x = e$

This implies that $x$ is having a self-inverse i.e. $x^{-1} = x$

Hence the question is asking to find the no. of element not having self-inverse.

$ herefore x^2 eq e$ means no. of element such that $x$ and $x^{-1}$ is DISTINCT.

 

If $x$ and $x^{-1}$ is DISTINCT then they exist in form of pairs.

$ herefore$ No. of element such that $x^2 eq e$ is EVEN

$ herefore $ Option “C” is INCORRECT and Option “D” is CORRECT.

FINAL ANSWER = { A: ✅, B: ❌, C: ❌, D: ✅}

 

Some Possible Variation:

  1. The number of elements $x$ of G such that $x^3=e$ excluding ‘e’ is  EVEN
  2. The number of elements $x$ of G such that $x^3 eq e $ is either EVEN or ODD (exclusively) 
  3. The number of elements $x$ of G such that $x^2 = e$ is either EVEN or ODD (exclusively)

Let $\mathrm{G}$ be a group.

Which of the following is/are true?

options.html: If for any $x, y, z$ in the group $\mathrm{G}, xy=zx$ implies $y=z$. Then $\mathrm{G}$ is Abelian.
If for any $x, y, z$ in the group $\text{G}, x y=x z$ implies $y=z$. Then $\text{G}$ is Abelian.
If for any $x, y, z$ in the group $\text{G}, y x=z x$ implies $y=z$. Then $\text{G}$ is Abelian.
If for any $x, y, z$ in the group $\mathrm{G}, yx= xz$ implies $y=z$. Then $\mathrm{G}$ is Abelian.

questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 4)

Detailed Video Solution: https://youtu.be/27dpP0LS00Q?t=1243

Option B is “Left Cancellation” property. It is satisfied by EVERY Group, abelian group or non-abelian group. So, the Left Cancellation property in a group doesn’t imply that it is Abelian(commutative).   

Option C is “Right Cancellation” property. It is satisfied by EVERY Group, abelian group or non-abelian group. So, the Right Cancellation property in a group doesn’t imply that it is Abelian(commutative).  

Option A is “Left-Right Cancellation” property. The Left-Right Cancellation property in a group implies that it is Abelian(commutative).   
Proof: https://youtu.be/27dpP0LS00Q?t=1243

Similarly, Option D is “Right-Left Cancellation” property. The Right-Left Cancellation property in a group implies that it is Abelian(commutative).

If he is a knave, then both 'p and q' of his statement becomes true, and it ends up being agsinst his knaves nature. So this case is a contradiction.

    If dueet is a knave : he should not tell a true statement. Here "Candy is a knave and I'm a knave" is a false statement, because it's in the form "p and q" and statement p is false here so overall statement is false. Everything falls into right places here.

\[

P(x,y) : x + y = 10

\]

\]
\[

\]

---

\[
\textbf{Option B: } \exists x\, \exists y\, P(x,y)
\]

\[
\text{There exist some } x,y \in \mathbb{Z} \text{ such that } x + y = 10
\]

\[
\text{True. Example: } x = 3,\ y = 7 \Rightarrow x + y = 10.
\]
---
\[
\textbf{Option C: } \forall x\, \forall y\, P(x,y)
\]

\[
\text{False. Counterexample: } x = 1,\ y = 1 \Rightarrow x + y = 2 \neq 10.
\]

---

\[
\textbf{Option D: } \exists x\, \forall y\, \neg P(x,y)
\]

\[
\text{False. For any } x \in \mathbb{Z}, \text{ choosing } y = 10 - x
\text{ makes } P(x,y) \text{ true.}
\]
---
\[
\boxed{\text{Correct answer: Option B}}
\]

questions.html:
Consider any set $A$ and predicate $P(x, y)$, which of the following statements are true?
(i) $\forall_{x \in A}  \forall_{y \in A} P(x, y) \rightarrow \exists_{x \in A} \exists_{ y \in A} P(x, y)$.
(ii) $\exists_{x \in A}  \exists_{y \in A}  P(x, y) \rightarrow \forall_{x \in A}  \forall_{y \in A}  P(x, y)$.
(iii) $\forall_{x \in A}  \exists_{y \in A}  P(x, y) \rightarrow \exists_{y \in A}  \forall_{x \in A}  P(x, y)$.
(iv) $\exists_{x \in A}  \forall_{y \in A}  P(x, y) \rightarrow \forall_{y \in A}  \exists_{x \in A}  P(x, y)$.
questions.solution:
Answer: Not available

Source solution 1 (score: 3)

Understand All types of Nested Quantifiers: https://youtu.be/bFfKD8o_5iU?feature=shared

(i) $\forall x \in A \, \forall y \in A \, P(x, y) \to \exists x \in A \, \exists y \in A \, P(x, y)$

  • $\forall x \, \forall y \, P(x, y)$ means $P(x,y)$ is true for all $x$ and $y$ in $A$.
  • $\exists x \, \exists y \, P(x, y)$ means there exist at least one $x$ and one $y$ in $A$ such that $P(x, y)$ is true.

If $P(x, y)$ is true for all $x$ and $y$, it must also be true for some $x$ and $y$.

Conclusion: True.

(ii) $\exists x \in A \, \exists y \in A \, P(x, y) \to \forall x \in A \, \forall y \in A \, P(x, y)$

  • $\exists x \, \exists y \, P(x, y)$ means $P(x, y)$ is true for at least one pair $(x, y)$ in $A$.
  • $\forall x \, \forall y \, P(x, y)$ means $P(x, y)$ is true for all pairs $(x, y)$ in $A$.

The existence of one $(x, y)$ satisfying $P(x, y)$ does not imply that $P(x, y)$ holds for all pairs.

Conclusion: False.

(iii) $\forall x \in A \, \exists y \in A \, P(x, y) \to \exists y \in A \, \forall x \in A \, P(x, y)$

 

  • $\forall x \, \exists y \, P(x, y)$ means for each $x$, there exists some $y$ such that $P(x, y)$ is true.
  • $\exists y \, \forall x \, P(x, y)$ means there exists a single $y$ such that $P(x, y)$ is true for all $x$.

The premise does not guarantee the conclusion. Each $x$ could have a different $y$ satisfying $P(x, y)$, and there may not be a single $y$ that works for all $x$.

Conclusion: False.

(iv) $\exists x \in A \, \forall y \in A \, P(x, y) \to \forall y \in A \, \exists x \in A \, P(x, y)$

 

  • $\exists x \, \forall y \, P(x, y)$ means there exists some $x$ such that $P(x, y)$ is true for all $y$.
  • $\forall y \, \exists x \, P(x, y)$ means for each $y$, there exists some $x$ such that $P(x, y)$ is true.

If $P(x, y)$ is true for one specific $x$ and all $y$, it follows that for any $y$, there is an $x$ (specifically, the same $x$) such that $P(x, y)$ holds.

Conclusion: True.
